questions.q: The chapter calls science 'a big adventure'. What three things does it say we do in this adventure?
questions.a: Ask questions, explore the world and try to understand how things work.
o: Ask questions, explore the world and try to understand how things work
Read books, memorise facts and repeat them correctly in tests
Collect objects, label them and keep them safe in a box
Watch experiments, copy the results and learn them by heart

questions.q: Four Grade 6 students describe their Sunday. Whose Sunday shows all three parts of the chapter's description of science: thinking, observing and doing?
questions.a: Ishita's: she observed the shadow, thought about why it changed and did something to follow it (marking its tip every hour). Kabir only memorised, Lalit only wondered and Meghna did none of the three.
o: Ishita watched the shadow of the water tank move during the day, wondered why, and put a stone at its tip every hour.
Kabir read a printed list of fifty science facts and learnt every one of them by heart for Monday's class quiz.
Lalit wondered why the Moon changes its shape from night to night, and then went to sleep without looking at it again.
Meghna sat on her terrace in the evening, enjoyed the cool breeze and listened to songs on the radio till dinner.

questions.q:
Read these statements about the chapter.
I. Science is a way of thinking, observing and doing things to understand the world we live in.
II. Science is found only in laboratories and in outer space.
III. There is always something new to discover, whether we study tiny grains of sand or massive mountains.
Which of these statements does the chapter support?
questions.a: I and III only. Statement II is wrong: the chapter says science is everywhere, from what is cooking in the kitchen to what is happening on the playground.
o: I and III only
I and II only
II and III only
I, II and III

questions.q:
Assertion (A): The chapter says that curiosity is the most important thing needed for doing science.
Reason (R): The title of this textbook, 'Curiosity', comes from this idea.
questions.a: Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A. The title comes from the idea that curiosity matters most; the title does not explain why curiosity is the most important thing.
o: Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
A is true but R is false.
A is false but R is true.

questions.q: True or False? The chapter says that science studies only very large things, such as massive mountains and vast forests. Give the verdict and the reason or the correction.
questions.a: False. The chapter says there is always something new and exciting to discover whether we study tiny grains of sand or massive mountains, a leaf of grass or a vast forest, so science studies very small things too.
s: States the verdict: False
Corrects it with a small thing named in the chapter, such as tiny grains of sand or a leaf of grass

questions.q: (a) Complete the chapter's description of science: 'Science is a way of ______, ______ and doing things.' (b) According to the chapter, what two things does science help us do?
questions.a: (a) thinking, observing. (b) It helps us understand the world we live in and uncover the secrets of the universe.
s: (a) Writes 'thinking' and 'observing'
(b) States understanding the world we live in and uncovering the secrets of the universe

questions.q: Sameer climbs the old stone steps of his school every day. (a) On Monday he counts the steps only because his teacher told him to, and then forgets about them. (b) On Tuesday he notices that the steps are worn smooth in the middle but not near the edges, and asks himself why. On which day does Sameer show curiosity in the chapter's sense? Give a reason from the chapter.
questions.a: On Tuesday. He notices something about his surroundings and asks why it is so; the chapter says curiosity, which leads us to ask questions and explore, is the most important thing for science. On Monday he only follows an instruction and asks no question.
s: Chooses Tuesday
Reason: he observes something and asks why, which is the curiosity the chapter says science starts with; Monday has no question of his own

questions.q: Give one example from the chapter for each of these: (a) a very small thing that science can study; (b) a mystery that the chapter says science helps us unravel; (c) a far-away place where science is found.
questions.a: (a) A tiny grain of sand (or a leaf of grass). (b) Why the stars shine (or how a flower knows when to open). (c) The depths of the ocean (or the vastness of outer space).
s: (a) Names a tiny grain of sand or a leaf of grass
(b) Names why the stars shine or how a flower knows when to open
(c) Names the depths of the ocean or the vastness of outer space

questions.q:
The nature club of a school in Shillong has Rs 2,800 for this term. Its members want to study something very small and something very large. A one-day bus trip to study a hill forest costs Rs 2,400. A hand lens, for looking closely at soil, grass and tiny insects in the school ground, costs Rs 150, and the club wants 4 lenses. One member says, 'Let us skip the lenses. The school ground has nothing new to discover; only big places like forests are worth studying.'
(a) What does the chapter say about studying tiny grains of sand compared with massive mountains?
(b) Can the club pay for the trip and all 4 lenses? Show the working.
(c) Is the member right about the school ground? Give a reason from the chapter.
(d) Suggest a plan within Rs 2,800 that still lets the club study something very small and something very large, and show that it fits the money.
questions.a: (a) Whether we study tiny grains of sand or massive mountains, a leaf of grass or a vast forest, there is always something new and exciting to discover. (b) No: 4 x 150 = Rs 600, and 2,400 + 600 = Rs 3,000, which is Rs 200 more than Rs 2,800. (c) No: the chapter says even tiny grains of sand and a leaf of grass have something new to discover, and that science is everywhere, so the school ground is worth studying too. (d) Go on the trip and buy 2 lenses to share: 2,400 + 2 x 150 = Rs 2,700, which is within Rs 2,800 (Rs 100 left). Keeping the trip, at most 2 lenses fit, since 3 lenses would make Rs 2,850.
s: (a) States that there is always something new to discover in tiny grains of sand as well as massive mountains
(b) Finds Rs 600 for the lenses and Rs 3,000 in all, Rs 200 over, so no
(c) Says the member is wrong, citing small things like sand or grass, or science being everywhere
(d) Gives the trip with at most 2 lenses (Rs 2,700) and checks it is within Rs 2,800

questions.q:
Four students each wrote one line for a class poster titled 'What is Science?'.
P: 'Science is a list of facts that we memorise for the exam.'
Q: 'Science is a way of thinking, observing and doing things to understand the world.'
R: 'Science happens only in big laboratories with special equipment.'
S: 'Science is asking questions about things around us, from a grain of sand to the stars, and trying to find out how they work.'
(i)-(iv) For each line P, Q, R and S, say whether it agrees with the chapter, with one reason.
(v) Neither Q nor S names the quality that the chapter calls the most important thing for doing science. Join Q and S into one line of at most 30 words that also includes that quality.
questions.a: (i) P does not agree: the chapter describes science as a way of thinking, observing and doing, and an adventure of asking and exploring, not a list of facts. (ii) Q agrees: it is the chapter's own description of science. (iii) R does not agree: the chapter says science is everywhere, from the kitchen to the playground, and great discoveries often come from unexpected places. (iv) S agrees: the chapter says we ask questions, explore and try to understand how things work, at every size from grains of sand to the stars. (v) Sample: 'Science is a way of thinking, observing and doing, driven by curiosity, in which we ask how things around us work, from a grain of sand to the stars.' (29 words; it must include curiosity.)
s: (i) P does not agree, with a reason (science is thinking, observing and doing, not a list of facts)
(ii) Q agrees, as the chapter's own description
(iii) R does not agree: science is everywhere, discoveries come from unexpected places
(iv) S agrees: asking questions and finding out how things work, small and large
(v) Writes one line of at most 30 words joining Q and S and including curiosity

questions.q: In the chapter's comparison of science with a jigsaw puzzle, what does each new discovery do?
questions.a: It adds another piece to the puzzle.
o: It adds another piece to the puzzle
It completes the whole puzzle
It removes a piece from the puzzle
It shows that the puzzle has no gaps left

questions.q: The chapter calls science a 'giant and ______ jigsaw puzzle'. Which word fills the gap and shows that this puzzle never gets finished?
questions.a: unending
o: unending
small
simple
fixed

questions.q: After a lesson on magnets, Arif notices that the magnet that keeps his pencil box shut and the magnet that holds a list on the fridge door seem to work in the same way. Which idea from the chapter's jigsaw passage does his discovery fit best?
questions.a: As we discover more and more, we start realising that ideas are all connected.
o: As we discover more and more, we start realising that ideas are all connected
Some pieces of the puzzle are put in the wrong place and must be moved
Every new discovery leaves fewer questions for us to find out about
Science is only about the things that we can find on planet Earth

questions.q:
Match each beginning from the chapter's jigsaw passage (1-4) with the ending the chapter gives it (A-D).
1. Every new discovery we make
2. Sometimes a piece of this puzzle
3. Every new piece of knowledge
4. As we discover more and more,
A. leads to more questions and more things to find out.
B. adds another piece to that puzzle.
C. we start realising that these ideas are all connected.
D. has been put in the wrong place and needs to be moved.

Assertion (A): Unlike a jigsaw puzzle bought from a shop, the puzzle of science can never be finished.
Reason (R): Every new piece of knowledge leads to more questions and more things to find out.
questions.a: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A. The chapter says there is no limit to what we can discover because every new piece of knowledge leads to more questions.
o: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true but R is false.
A is false but R is true.

questions.q: True or False? According to the chapter, an idea in science that people once accepted can later be changed. Give the verdict and the reason.
questions.a: True. The chapter says that sometimes a piece of the science puzzle has been put in the wrong place and needs to be moved, because new discoveries often change our understanding of the world.
s: States the verdict: True
Reason: a wrongly placed piece is moved; new discoveries often change our understanding

questions.q: (a) What does the chapter compare science to? (b) Why does the chapter say there is no limit to what we can discover?
questions.a: (a) A giant and unending jigsaw puzzle. (b) Because every new piece of knowledge leads to more questions and more things to find out.
s: (a) Names a giant, unending jigsaw puzzle
(b) Every new piece of knowledge leads to more questions and things to find out

questions.q:
Say which idea from the chapter's jigsaw passage each event shows.
(a) Class 6 had written that the guava tree in their school gives fruit only in winter. After keeping a record for a whole year, they found that it also gives fruit in the rainy season, so they changed their note.
(b) Finding out why the classroom fan makes a noise leads the class to two new questions about the fan.
(c) Nidhi finds that what she learnt at home about keeping biscuits dry helps her understand why her school keeps chalk in a closed box.
questions.a: (a) A piece was in the wrong place and was moved: a new discovery changed their understanding. (b) Every new piece of knowledge leads to more questions and more things to find out. (c) As we discover more, we start realising that ideas are all connected.
s: (a) A wrongly placed piece is moved; new discoveries change our understanding
(b) New knowledge leads to more questions
(c) Ideas are all connected

questions.q:
Vinay tries a new comparison: 'Science is like climbing a staircase. Each discovery is one more step up, and when we reach the top step, science is complete.' Compare his staircase with the chapter's jigsaw puzzle.
(a) Give one way in which the staircase matches the jigsaw puzzle.
(b) Which idea of the jigsaw puzzle does 'reaching the top step' go against? Explain.
(c) A jigsaw piece may be found in the wrong place and moved. Can the staircase show this? Explain.
(d) Decide which comparison describes science better, with a reason.
questions.a: (a) Each step, like each new jigsaw piece, stands for a new discovery that adds to what we know. (b) It goes against the puzzle being unending: the chapter says there is no limit to what we can discover, because every new piece of knowledge leads to more questions, so there is no top step. (c) No: a step once climbed stays where it is, but the chapter says new discoveries often change our understanding, so a piece sometimes has to be moved. (d) The jigsaw puzzle is better, because it shows both that science never ends and that ideas can be corrected, which the staircase cannot show.
s: (a) Each step, like each piece, is a new discovery added
(b) The top step goes against the unending puzzle: new knowledge leads to more questions
(c) No: the staircase cannot show a wrong piece being moved when understanding changes
(d) Chooses the jigsaw puzzle, giving that it shows no end and correction

questions.q:
In 2015, Class 6 of a school in Jaipur wrote a booklet, 'Our School Garden', with 24 statements based on what they saw. In 2025, a new Class 6 checked each statement by watching the garden for a year. They found that 15 statements still held, 6 had to be changed after better observations, and 3 could not be checked yet. The checking also gave them 14 new questions.
(i) What fraction of the 24 statements still held? Give it in its simplest form.
(ii) Which idea from the chapter's jigsaw passage do the 6 changed statements show?
(iii) Which idea do the 14 new questions show?
(iv) The principal suggests throwing the 2015 booklet away, because 9 of its 24 statements were not confirmed. Is this a good decision? Use the numbers and the chapter.
(v) What should the class do with the 3 statements that could not be checked yet?
questions.a: (i) 15/24 = 5/8. (ii) A piece put in the wrong place is moved: new discoveries change our understanding. (iii) Every new piece of knowledge leads to more questions and more things to find out. (iv) No: 15 of 24 (5/8, more than half) still hold; only 6 were found wrong, and the 3 unchecked ones are not proved wrong (6 + 3 = 9). In the chapter's puzzle a wrongly placed piece is moved, not the whole puzzle thrown away, so the class should correct the 6 statements and keep the rest. (v) Keep them as open questions and check them later with more observations, since science goes on finding out.
s: (ii) Names the idea of a wrongly placed piece being moved as understanding changes
(iii) Names the idea that new knowledge leads to more questions
(iv) Decides no, using 15 of 24 held, 6 wrong and 3 unchecked, and that wrong pieces are moved, not the puzzle thrown away
(v) Keeps the 3 as open questions to test later by more observations

questions.q: In the chapter's list of things in our pencil box, what does the magnet do?
questions.a: It keeps the box closed.
o: It keeps the box closed
It holds the pencils in a row
It keeps the eraser clean
It stops the ruler from bending

questions.q:
Anu wrote five questions.
P: How can we tell how hot the bath water is?
Q: What is a metal key made of?
R: Why does water become ice when we cool it?
S: How does a caterpillar turn into a butterfly?
T: Why do we enjoy a warm shower in winter?
How many of her questions belong to the chapter's preview of water and hot and cold?
questions.a: Three (P, R and T). Q belongs with materials, and S with how plants and animals grow.

questions.q: Four students summarise what the chapter says about life on Earth. Which summary misreads the chapter?
questions.a: Ravi's summary, that all plants and animals live in the same kind of region, misreads it: the chapter says they have managed to survive and thrive in different regions of the planet.
o: Ravi: 'All plants and animals on Earth live in the same kind of region.'
Sita: 'Earth is the only planet that we know supports life.'
Joel: 'Earth has an environment that we must protect.'
Fatima: 'Plants and animals survive and thrive in different regions.'

questions.q:
Read these statements about the chapter's preview.
I. The chapter says Earth is the only planet we know that supports life.
II. The chapter says India, a large and diverse country, has different cuisines with many tasty dishes.
III. The chapter explains why and how it rains.
Which of these statements are correct?
questions.a: I and II only. Statement III is wrong: the chapter only asks why and how it rains; it does not explain it.
o: I and II only
I and III only
II and III only
I, II and III

questions.q:
Assertion (A): The chapter asks, 'How do we separate different materials from one another?'
Reason (R): The chapter says that the paper, the metal key, the plastic ruler and the rubber eraser in our box are all made of the same material.
questions.a: A is true but R is false. The chapter asks whether these things are made of different materials; it never says they are all made of the same material.
o: A is true but R is false.
Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is false but R is true.

questions.q: True or False? In the chapter's preview, a seed growing into a plant and a caterpillar turning into a butterfly are both examples that lead to the same question: how do plants and animals grow? Give the verdict and the reason.
questions.a: True. The chapter mentions seeing a seed grow into a plant and a caterpillar transform into a butterfly, and then asks how these plants and animals grow.
s: States the verdict: True
Reason: the chapter gives both observations and then asks how plants and animals grow

questions.q: The chapter lists many things around us and asks what they are made of. Name any four of these things.
questions.a: Any four of: the paper we write on, the metal key, the plastic ruler, the rubber eraser, the magnet that keeps the box closed, the clothes we wear, the cup we drink milk in.
s: Names any two things from the chapter's list
Names two more things from the list

questions.q: Write one question that the chapter's preview asks about each of these: (a) the dishes we eat; (b) water; (c) the things around us, such as a ruler and an eraser.
questions.a: (a) What are they made of? or How do we find out? (b) Why and how does it rain? or How do we understand hot and cold? (c) What are they made of? Are they made of different materials? or How do we separate different materials from one another?
s: (a) Gives a food question from the chapter: what are the dishes made of, or how do we find out
(b) Gives a water question from the chapter: why and how it rains, or how we understand hot and cold
(c) Gives a materials question: what they are made of, or how we separate materials

questions.q:
Place each student question under the part of the chapter's preview it belongs to, and give a reason.
(a) 'How did the small tamarind seed we planted become a plant taller than me?'
(b) 'Sand got mixed into the rice at home. How could we get the sand out?'
(c) 'Why does the water in a pan turn into steam when Amma keeps it on the stove for a long time?'
questions.a: (a) Growth of plants and animals on Earth: like the chapter's seed growing into a plant, it asks how a plant grows. (b) Materials: the chapter asks how we separate different materials from one another, and sand and rice are different materials. (c) Water: the chapter's water part notes that water boils and becomes steam when we heat it.
s: (a) Growth of plants and animals, with the seed example as reason
(b) Materials, because it is about separating different materials
(c) Water, because it is about water becoming steam when heated

questions.q:
Class 6B of a school in Pune listed the 40 things in their classroom by the main material each is made of: wood 14, metal 11, plastic 9, glass 4 and rubber 2. Their teacher reminded them of the chapter's questions about the things around us, such as the metal key and the rubber eraser in our box.
(a) Write two questions that the chapter asks about such things.
(b) Which material is used for the most things in the list?
(c) How many of the 40 things are made of metal or plastic?
(d) The class can study only two materials this month and wants to cover as many of the 40 things as it can. Which two materials should it choose, and how many things will they cover?
questions.a: (a) Any two of: What are they made of? Are they made of different materials? How do we separate different materials from one another? (b) Wood (14 things). (c) 11 + 9 = 20 things. (d) Wood and metal, the two largest groups: 14 + 11 = 25 things.
s: (a) Writes two of the chapter's questions about materials
(b) Names wood (14)
(c) Finds 11 + 9 = 20
(d) Chooses wood and metal and finds 25 things

questions.q: In the chapter's list of steps of the scientific method, what do we do right after we guess a possible answer to our question?
questions.a: We test the guess through experiments or more observations.
o: We test the guess through experiments or more observations
We observe something that we find interesting
We think of a question about what we saw
We stop, because the guess is the final answer

questions.q: In the chapter's pen example, how is the first guess, that the ink has finished, tested?
questions.a: By opening the pen and checking the ink refill.
o: By opening the pen and checking the ink refill
By buying a new pen and writing with it
By asking a friend why pens stop writing
By shaking the pen hard several times

questions.q: Yusuf's football does not bounce as high as it used to. He wonders why and guesses that it has lost some air. He pumps air into it and drops it from the same height as before, and now it bounces much higher. When he analyses this result, what should he conclude?
questions.a: The result supports his guess that the ball had lost air.
o: The result supports his guess that the ball had lost air
The result shows his guess was wrong, so he needs a new guess
The result means nothing, because he did not use a laboratory
The result proves that every ball that bounces low has lost air

questions.q:
Leela's notes on a pot of bean seeds are given below (1-4). Match each note with the step of the scientific method it shows (A-D).
1. Three of the eight bean seeds in my pot have not sprouted after a week.
2. Why have only these three not sprouted?
3. Maybe I planted these three too deep in the soil.
4. I plant three new seeds close to the top and watch them for a week.
A. Guess
B. Observe
C. Test
D. Question

Assertion (A): In the pen example, finding that the ink refill is empty tells us that the guess 'the ink has finished' was correct.
Reason (R): In the scientific method, we test a guess before we make it.
questions.a: A is true but R is false. The chapter says that if the refill is empty, the guess was correct; but in its steps we first guess a possible answer and then test the guess.
o: A is true but R is false.
Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is false but R is true.

questions.q: Write the five steps of the scientific method in the order the chapter gives them.
questions.a: Observe something interesting or not understood; wonder and think of a question about it; guess a possible answer; test the guess through experiments or more observations; analyse the results to see if they answer the question.
s: Gives the first three steps in order: observe, question, guess
Gives the last two steps in order: test the guess, then analyse the results

questions.q: Rekha's kite keeps diving to the ground although a good wind is blowing. (a) Write one guess she could make about why the kite dives. (b) Describe a test that would check that guess.
questions.a: Sample: (a) The tail of the kite is too short. (b) Tie on a longer tail and fly the kite again in the same wind, and see whether it still dives. Any guess about a possible cause is accepted if the test checks that same guess.
s: (a) Gives a guess about a possible cause that can be checked
(b) Gives a test, by an experiment or more observations, that checks that same guess

questions.q: In the chapter's pen example, write: (a) the question you ask yourself when your pen stops writing; (b) the second guess you make when you find that the ink has not finished; (c) the name the chapter gives to this way of finding out.
questions.a: (a) 'Why did my pen stop writing?' (b) The ink might have dried up. (c) The scientific method.
s: (a) Writes 'Why did my pen stop writing?'
(b) States that the ink might have dried up
(c) Names the scientific method

questions.q:
Ishaan's chapati in his lunch box becomes hard and dry by lunch time. He wonders why, and guesses that the lid of his box is loose. To test this, he packs one chapati in his usual box and one in a box with a tight lid. By lunch time both chapatis are equally hard and dry.
(a) Write Ishaan's observation and his question.
(b) What does the result tell him about his guess? Explain.
(c) In the chapter's pen example, what is done when the first guess turns out to be wrong? What should Ishaan do now?
(d) Suggest one new guess Ishaan could make, and a test for it.
questions.a: (a) Observation: his chapati becomes hard and dry by lunch time. Question: Why does my chapati become hard and dry? (b) The result does not support his guess: the chapati in the tight box dried just as much, so a loose lid is not the reason. (c) In the pen example, when the refill is not empty, another guess is made (the ink might have dried up) and tested in a different way; Ishaan too should make a new guess and test it. (d) Sample: guess that the chapati dries because it lies uncovered on the plate for a long time before packing; test by packing one chapati straight away and one after leaving it out, and comparing them at lunch. Any testable guess with a matching test is accepted.
s: (a) States the observation and a why-question about it
(b) Says the guess is not supported, because both chapatis dried equally
(c) States that another guess is made and tested, and that Ishaan should do the same
(d) Gives a new guess and a test that checks it

questions.q:
Tara notices that many mustard seeds in her school's seed tray did not sprout. She guesses that they were given too much water. She takes 4 trays with 10 seeds each, keeps them in the same place, and gives each tray a different amount of water every day. After a week:
Tray A, no water: 0 seeds sprouted
Tray B, 1 spoon a day: 7 sprouted
Tray C, 3 spoons a day: 9 sprouted
Tray D, 6 spoons a day: 4 sprouted
(i) Name the observation and the question that started Tara's work.
(ii) Which step of the scientific method are the four trays?
(iii) Which tray did best, and what percentage of its seeds sprouted?
(iv) Do the results support her guess? Use the numbers.
(v) Her friend says, 'This proves that too much water is the only reason seeds fail to sprout.' Is the friend right? Give two reasons from the results.
questions.a: (i) Observation: many mustard seeds in the tray did not sprout. Question: Why did these seeds not sprout? (ii) Testing the guess (an experiment). (iii) Tray C: 9 of 10 = 90%. (iv) Yes, partly: with 6 spoons only 4 sprouted, fewer than the 9 with 3 spoons, so too much water does seem to lower sprouting. (v) No. Tray A, with no water at all, had 0 sprouts, so too little water also stops seeds sprouting; and even Tray C had 1 seed that did not sprout, so there may be other reasons. With only one tray of 10 seeds for each amount, more tests are needed before anything is proved.
s: (i) States the observation (seeds did not sprout) and a why-question
(ii) Names the trays as the test of her guess
(iii) Names Tray C and finds 90%
(iv) Says the results support the guess in part, comparing 4 sprouts at 6 spoons with 9 at 3 spoons
(v) Says the friend is wrong, giving two reasons such as Tray A's 0 sprouts, the one seed that failed in Tray C, or too few trays

questions.q: In the chapter, what is the bicycle repair person trying to find out about the flat tyre?
questions.a: From where the air leaked out.
o: From where the air leaked out
How old the tyre is
Who rode the bicycle last
Which colour the new tyre should be

questions.q: Mr Gill's scooter will not start. He guesses that the petrol has run out, checks the tank, and finds it nearly full. Following the way of working shown in the chapter's pen example, what should he do next?
questions.a: Make another guess about the cause and test it.
o: Make another guess about the cause and test it
Decide that the scooter can never be repaired
Keep checking the petrol tank again and again
Accept 'no petrol' as the answer, since it was his first guess

questions.q: Ruchi's table fan does not run when she plugs it into the bedroom socket. She thinks the fault is either in the fan or in the bedroom socket. Test 1: she plugs the fan into the kitchen socket, which works for the mixer; the fan still does not run. Test 2: she plugs a lamp into the bedroom socket; the lamp lights. What should she conclude?
questions.a: The fault is in the fan, not in the bedroom socket: the fan fails even in a working socket, and the bedroom socket works for the lamp.
o: The fault is in the fan, not in the bedroom socket
The fault is in the bedroom socket, not in the fan
Both the fan and the bedroom socket are faulty
The two tests disagree, so nothing can be concluded

questions.q:
Read these statements about the chapter.
I. The chapter says the bicycle repair person wonders whether the tyre is too old.
II. The chapter says learning science will develop our capabilities for finding solutions to bigger problems.
III. The chapter says scientists across the world work together, often in large teams.
Which of these statements are correct?
questions.a: II and III only. Statement I is wrong: the repair person asks from where the air leaked out.
o: II and III only
I and II only
I and III only
I, II and III

questions.q:
Assertion (A): A cook who wonders whether too much water made the dal spill out of the cooker is working like a scientist.
Reason (R): The chapter says that anyone who follows the scientific method is working like a scientist.
questions.a: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A. The cook observes the spill and asks a question with a possible answer, which is following the scientific method.
o: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true but R is false.
A is false but R is true.

questions.q: True or False? In the chapter, the electrician tries to find out whether the light bulb is not working because of a problem in the wiring of the whole house. Give the verdict and the correct statement.
questions.a: False. The chapter's electrician tries to find out whether the problem is with the bulb or with the switch.
s: States the verdict: False
Correct statement: the electrician asks whether the problem is with the bulb or the switch

questions.q: (a) Who are scientists, according to the chapter? (b) The chapter says other people can also work like scientists. What must such a person do?
questions.a: (a) People who follow the scientific method to solve problems or to discover new things. (b) Follow the scientific method: observe, ask a question, guess, test the guess and analyse the result.
s: (a) People who follow the scientific method to solve problems or discover new things
(b) Anyone who follows the scientific method works like a scientist

questions.q: Neeraj says: 'The cook, the bicycle repair person and the electrician in the chapter are not really like scientists, because none of them works in a laboratory or does a big experiment.' Is Neeraj's claim right? Give your verdict and two reasons from the chapter.
questions.a: No. The chapter says anyone who follows the scientific method is working like a scientist, wherever they are. Each of the three observes a problem and asks a question with a possible answer (too much water? where did the air leak out? the bulb or the switch?), and the chapter says a guess can be tested through experiments or more observations, so checking a tyre or a bulb is a real test.
s: Verdict: the claim is wrong
Reason: anyone who follows the scientific method works like a scientist, wherever they are
Reason: a test can be more observations, not only a laboratory experiment; each of the three asks a question and checks it

questions.a: (a) No water comes out of the hose when the tap is opened. (b) Why is no water coming out of the hose? (c) Sample: the hose is bent and pressed flat somewhere. (d) Sample: straighten the hose along its whole length and open the tap again. (Another sample: guess the tap has no water; test by taking the hose off and opening the tap.) (e) Make another guess and test it, as in the pen example.
s: (a) States the observation: no water comes out of the hose
(b) Writes a why-question about it
(c) Gives a possible cause as a guess
(d) Gives a test that checks that guess
(e) Says she should make another guess and test it

questions.q:
The cook in a school canteen in Lucknow finds that the rice sometimes sticks and burns at the bottom of the pot. He guesses that he is adding too little water. For one week he cooks the same amount of rice each day and notes:
Monday: 4 cups of water, high flame, burnt
Tuesday: 5 cups of water, high flame, burnt
Wednesday: 4 cups of water, low flame, not burnt
Thursday: 5 cups of water, low flame, not burnt
Friday: 4 cups of water, high flame, burnt
(a) What did the cook observe, and what was his guess?
(b) On how many days did the rice burn, and what was the flame on each of those days?
(c) Do the results support his guess about too little water? Explain using Tuesday and Wednesday.
(d) What should the cook change from next week? Justify it with the data.
questions.a: (a) He observed that the rice sometimes sticks and burns at the bottom of the pot; his guess was that he adds too little water. (b) 3 days (Monday, Tuesday and Friday), and the flame was high on all three. (c) No: on Tuesday he used more water (5 cups) and the rice still burnt, while on Wednesday he used less water (4 cups) and it did not burn, so the amount of water did not decide the burning. (d) Cook on a low flame: both low-flame days (Wednesday and Thursday) were not burnt and all three high-flame days were burnt, whether he used 4 or 5 cups.
s: (a) States the observation (rice burns at the bottom) and the guess (too little water)
(b) Finds 3 days, all on a high flame
(c) Says no, using Tuesday (more water, burnt) and Wednesday (less water, not burnt)
(d) Decides on a low flame, using the pattern of all five days

questions.q: At the end of the chapter, science is compared with children enjoying something, to show that science is joyful exploration. What are the children enjoying?
questions.a: The rain.
o: The rain
A cricket match
A school holiday
A birthday party

questions.q: According to the chapter, what is the first and foremost thing needed to learn science well?
questions.a: To be curious and observe your surroundings keenly.
o: To be curious and observe your surroundings keenly
To own a microscope and other costly equipment
To memorise every definition in the book
To always find every answer on your own

questions.q: Activity 1.3 in the chapter asks you to write a 'Why?' question about something, and then write how you would try to find an answer. Which student's entry does both parts of the activity?
questions.a: Harsh's entry: it asks a why-question and also says how he would try to find the answer.
o: Harsh: 'Why does bread on our shelf go mouldy faster in damp weather? I will keep one slice in a dry tin and one in a damp place and check both daily.'
Pallavi: 'Why does bread go mouldy on our kitchen shelf? Somebody must already know the answer, so I will not think about it any more.'
Arjun: 'Bread is soft and brown. We eat it at breakfast every day, and my little brother likes it with jam more than with butter.'
Sana: 'I will keep two slices of bread on our kitchen shelf, one in a tin and one on a plate, and look at both of them every day.'

questions.q:
Match each line from the end of the chapter (1-4) with what it tells a student (A-D).
1. 'Science is rarely done alone.'
2. 'You will not find answers to all your questions in Grade 6.'
3. 'Much like children enjoying the rain'
4. 'To be a wise person, you must be a "whys" person!'
A. Science is joyful exploration.
B. Keep asking why about things.
C. Ask friends for help; it is more fun to discover together.
D. Do not worry; the journey of science goes on for years.

Assertion (A): The chapter tells Grade 6 students not to worry if they cannot find answers to all their questions this year.
Reason (R): The chapter says that to learn science well, the first and foremost thing is to be curious and observe your surroundings keenly.
questions.a: Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A. The chapter's reason for not worrying is that students are starting a journey of science for the next five years or even beyond.
o: Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
A is true but R is false.
A is false but R is true.

questions.q: True or False? The chapter says that a student will find the answers to all her science questions by the end of Grade 6. Give the verdict and the correct statement.
questions.a: False. The chapter says you will not find answers to all your questions in Grade 6, and that you are starting a journey of science for the next five years or even beyond.
s: States the verdict: False
Correct statement: not all questions are answered in Grade 6; the journey goes on for five years or more

questions.q: (a) How do scientists across the world usually work, according to the chapter? (b) What does the chapter advise you to do if you cannot find an answer by yourself?
questions.a: (a) They work together, often in large teams; science is rarely done alone. (b) Ask your friends to help you out, because it is more fun to discover things together.
s: (a) Scientists work together, often in large teams
(b) Ask friends to help

questions.q: Tanvir writes: 'Asking questions that we cannot answer only makes us feel stuck. So it is better to ask only those questions whose answers are already in our book.' Is Tanvir's idea in line with the chapter? Give your verdict and two ideas from the last two pages of the chapter.
questions.a: No. The chapter says the world is full of things we do not know that are waiting to be explored, and that we will not find answers to all our questions in Grade 6 because science is a journey for the next five years or even beyond. It also says that if we cannot find an answer ourselves we can ask friends, and that we should never stop wondering and asking questions.
s: Verdict: not in line with the chapter
One idea: unanswered questions are expected; the world is full of things waiting to be explored, and the journey goes beyond Grade 6
Second idea: ask friends for help, or never stop wondering and asking questions

questions.q:
A teacher in Kochi asked the 40 students of Class 6A: 'What do you do when you cannot find the answer to a question you asked?' Their answers: 18 said they feel worried, 12 said they give up and forget the question, 6 said they write it down to come back to later, and 4 said they ask friends to work on it with them.
(a) What does the chapter say to a student who cannot find answers to all her questions in Grade 6?
(b) How many of the 40 students already keep their questions alive or ask friends, as the chapter advises? What percentage is that?
(c) Which group of students is acting most against the chapter's advice never to stop wondering?
(d) The teacher has time for one plan. Plan X: she answers every open question herself at once. Plan Y: she sets up a 'Question Shelf' where students pin open questions and work on them with friends. Which plan fits the chapter better? Justify with the chapter and the numbers.
questions.a: (a) Do not worry: you are starting a journey of science for the next five years or even beyond. (b) 6 + 4 = 10 students, which is 10/40 = 25%. (c) The 12 who give up and forget the question. (d) Plan Y: the chapter says science is rarely done alone, that it is more fun to discover things together, and that we should keep exploring and never stop wondering. Plan Y moves the 30 students (18 + 12, that is 75%) who worry or give up towards what the 10 already do, while Plan X would end the questions instead of keeping students exploring.
s: (a) States the chapter's advice: do not worry, the journey continues beyond Grade 6
(b) Finds 10 students and 25%
(c) Names the 12 who give up and forget
(d) Chooses Plan Y with a reason from the chapter (teamwork, keep wondering) and the numbers (30 of 40 worry or give up)

questions.q:
Your cousin Meher is about to start Grade 6 and has three worries about Science. Reply to each worry using the chapter, then help her begin.
(i) 'We have no laboratory at home, so I cannot learn science.'
(ii) 'Last month I asked three "why" questions and could not answer any of them, so I must be bad at science.'
(iii) 'Science is only hard work, with no fun in it.'
(iv) Suggest one thing in her home or street that she could be curious about, and write a 'why' question on it.
(v) Write how she could try to find the answer to that question.
questions.a: (i) The chapter says the first and foremost thing for learning science well is to be curious and observe your surroundings keenly; she needs curiosity, not a laboratory. (ii) The chapter says you will not find answers to all your questions in Grade 6; she is starting a journey of science for the next five years or even beyond, and she can ask friends for help. (iii) The chapter says science is all about joyful exploration, much like children enjoying the rain. (iv) Sample: 'Why do the leaves of the mango tree in our street look dusty near the road but clean at the back?' (v) Sample: guess that passing vehicles raise the dust, then look at the leaves on both sides on a few days and compare. Any why-question with a matching way to find out is accepted.
s: (i) Replies that curiosity and keen observation, not a laboratory, come first
(ii) Replies that not all questions are answered in Grade 6; the journey continues, and friends can help
(iii) Replies that science is joyful exploration, like children enjoying the rain
(iv) Writes a why-question about something in her surroundings
(v) Describes a way to find the answer, such as a guess and a test
